pos: v. (past tense; broken, transgressed, done violence to)
etymology: From Latin violare, to treat with violence, related to vis, force. The Hebrew chamas means to do violence or wrong.
biblical_def: Ezekiel 22 is a catalogue of Jerusalem's sins, class by class: princes, priests, prophets and people. Of the priests God says: “Her priests have violated my law, and have profaned mine holy things: they have put no difference between the holy and profane, neither have they shewed difference between the unclean and the clean, and have hid their eyes from my sabbaths, and I am profaned among them.” The priests' office was to teach Israel to distinguish holy from common and clean from unclean (Leviticus 10:10). Instead they did violence to God's law, erasing the very distinctions they were appointed to guard. The result was that God Himself was profaned among His people. The verse shows that the deepest corruption of a nation begins with the corruption of its teachers. “For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts” (Malachi 2:7). When ministers blur the line between holy and profane, the whole people loses its sense of God. The chapter ends with God seeking a man to stand in the gap, and finding none (Ezekiel 22:30), a need met only in Christ.

And that ye may put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean;
Mal 2:7

corruption_summary: Ministers blur the distinction between holy and profane in worship, doctrine and life, presenting the erasure of God's boundaries as relevance or inclusion.
corruption_paragraphs: The priests of Ezekiel's day have modern successors: ministers who erase the line between the church and the world, between sacred worship and entertainment, between what God calls clean and what He calls unclean. The erasure is often presented as relevance, openness or compassion.

God's verdict is that such teachers do violence to His law and profane His name. The pastor's office is to teach the difference between the holy and the profane, and to guard the regulative principle in worship and the moral law in life. When the teachers fail, the people lose their sense of God.

etymology: From Old English spillan, to destroy or squander, later to let a liquid run out. The Hebrew word means poured out or flowing down.
biblical_def: Joab, seeing that King David longed for his banished son Absalom, sent a wise woman of Tekoa to speak to the king in a parable. Her climactic words were these: “For we must needs die, and are as water spilt on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again; neither doth God respect any person: yet doth he devise means, that his banished be not expelled from him.” The first half is a sober truth about mortality: life once poured out cannot be gathered back. The second half is a gospel truth, even though the woman spoke it to serve Joab's political purpose: God devises means to bring His banished home. David recalled Absalom without requiring repentance, and the result was rebellion. But God's means of restoring the banished is not an indulgent pardon that ignores sin. He devised the costliest means of all: the death of His own Son, whose blood was poured out like water (Psalm 22:14), so that sinners exiled by their guilt could be brought near. In Christ, God is both “just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SPILL, to suffer to fall or run out of a vessel; to lose or suffer to be scattered; to shed; SPILT, shed; suffered to be lost.

To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.
corruption_summary: God's mercy to the banished is reduced to indulgent pardon without repentance or atonement, the very pattern David followed with Absalom to his sorrow.
corruption_paragraphs: The woman of Tekoa's plea worked on David's feelings, and he recalled Absalom without justice or repentance. Modern theology often imagines God's mercy the same way: a sentimental welcome that sets aside His justice. That idea produces rebellion, not reconciliation.

The gospel shows God devising means that satisfy justice and display mercy together. The banished are brought home through the blood of Christ, and those brought home are changed. God is just and the justifier of him that believeth in Jesus.

etymology: From Old French haler, to pull or drag, of Germanic origin, the same root as haul. Luke's Greek suro means to drag.
biblical_def: After the stoning of Stephen, a great persecution arose against the church at Jerusalem. Luke records its chief agent: “As for Saul, he made havock of the church, entering into every house, and haling men and women committed them to prison.” Saul did not merely oppose the Christians in debate; he dragged them from their homes, women as well as men, and threw them into prison. Later he confessed, “I persecuted this way unto the death” (Acts 22:4) and “beyond measure I persecuted the church of God, and wasted it” (Galatians 1:13). Yet this same man was arrested by the risen Christ on the road to Damascus and became the apostle to the Gentiles. His conversion is the supreme example of sovereign grace: the persecutor became the preacher, not because he sought Christ but because Christ sought him. Paul himself drew the lesson: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief” (1 Timothy 1:15). The persecution also scattered the church, and “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Acts 8:4). God turned the haling of His saints into the spread of His gospel.

corruption_summary: Saul's conversion is psychologized as the resolution of inner conflict, rather than the sovereign intervention of the risen Christ in the life of an active persecutor.
corruption_paragraphs: Some modern interpreters explain Paul's conversion as a psychological crisis, guilt over Stephen's death or tension with the law resolving itself in a vision. The text leaves no room for this: Saul was still breathing out threatenings and slaughter when Christ met him.

The Reformed doctrine of effectual calling finds its classic illustration here. The persecutor did not choose Christ; Christ chose and called him. His case gives hope that no sinner is beyond the reach of sovereign grace, and it shows God using even persecution to spread His Word.

pos: n. (animal fat; a soft, oily substance)
etymology: From Old French graisse, fat, from Latin crassus, thick or fat. The Hebrew cheleb means fat, the same word used of the fat of sacrifices.
biblical_def: The longest psalm is a meditation on the Word of God, and in its ninth section the psalmist contrasts himself with the proud: “Their heart is as fat as grease; but I delight in thy law.” A heart fat as grease is insensible, dull and unresponsive. In Scripture, fatness of heart is a picture of spiritual stupor brought on by prosperity and pride; Isaiah was told, “Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes” (Isaiah 6:10). The proud had forged lies against the psalmist, but their hearts could feel nothing of God's Word. The psalmist's heart, by contrast, had been made tender through suffering: “It is good for me that I have been afflicted; that I might learn thy statutes” (Psalm 119:71). The contrast teaches that affliction is often God's instrument for keeping the heart soft, and that ease and prosperity can encase the soul in a deadening layer of self-satisfaction. The remedy for a greasy heart is the Word of God applied by the Spirit, which alone can make a stony heart into a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26).

webster_full: GREASE, n. Animal fat in a soft state; oily or unctuous matter of any kind, as tallow, lard.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word keeps its plain sense.

Comfortable affluence is the native soil of the greasy heart. Believers in prosperous lands should take warning: ease can encase the soul in insensibility to God. The psalmist learned to say that affliction was good for him, because it made him learn God's statutes. Delight in the law is the mark of a heart God has softened.

pos: v.i. (to look steadily and with curiosity)
etymology: From Middle English gasen, probably of Scandinavian origin, related to Swedish dialect gasa, to stare. The Hebrew raah is the ordinary verb to see.
biblical_def: When God descended on Mount Sinai in fire, smoke and trembling, He commanded strict bounds around the mountain. Then He sent Moses down again with an urgent warning: “And the LORD said unto Moses, Go down, charge the people, lest they break through unto the LORD to gaze, and many of them perish.” Curiosity is not reverence. To press forward to gaze at the holy God as at a spectacle would be to treat His presence as an object of entertainment, and the penalty was death. Hebrews recalls the terror of Sinai: “And if so much as a beast touch the mountain, it shall be stoned” (Hebrews 12:20), and then declares that believers have come not to that mount but to mount Sion, to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant. Through Christ believers may draw near with boldness. Yet the conclusion of Hebrews is not casualness: “let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear: For our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:28-29). Access through Christ does not abolish holiness; it makes it possible for sinners to approach without perishing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): GAZE, to fix the eyes and look steadily and earnestly; to look with eagerness or curiosity, as in admiration, astonishment, or in study.
webster_full: GAZE, v.i. To fix the eyes and look steadily and earnestly.
To look with eagerness or curiosity, as in admiration, astonishment or study.

(For they could not endure that which was commanded, And if so much as a beast touch the mountain, it shall be stoned, or thrust through with a dart:
corruption_summary: Worship is turned into spectacle, God's presence treated as an experience to be gazed at and consumed rather than approached with reverence through Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Much contemporary worship is staged for the curious onlooker, with lights, smoke and performance designed to produce an experience. The instinct to gaze at the holy as spectacle is the very thing God forbade at Sinai.

The gospel opens a way into God's presence through the blood of Christ, but that way calls for reverence and godly fear, not entertainment. The regulative principle guards the church from turning worship into spectacle and keeps it centred on Word, prayer, praise and ordinances as God commands.

etymology: From Old English lanu, a narrow way or passage, related to Dutch laan, an avenue. Luke's Greek rhume means a narrow street or alley.
biblical_def: In the parable of the great supper, a certain man made a great feast and bade many. When all was ready, the invited guests began with one consent to make excuse: a piece of ground, five yoke of oxen, a new wife. The master was angry and said to his servant, “Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind.” When there was still room, he sent him further: “Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled” (Luke 14:23). The parable was spoken at a Pharisee's table. The first guests are those who presumed on their privileges and despised the invitation; the poor of the lanes are the outcasts of Israel; the travellers of the highways and hedges are the Gentiles. The compelling is not force of arms but the urgency of gospel persuasion. The supper will be full, for God's house will be filled with all whom He has called. The lanes of the city represent the places respectable religion overlooks, where the gospel finds the guests who know they have nothing to bring.

webster_full: LANE, n. A narrow way or passage, or a private passage, as distinguished from a public road or highway.

And they all with one consent began to make excuse. The first said unto him, I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused.

corruption_summary: The parable is flattened into a lesson in social inclusion, losing its gospel point: the invited despised the feast, and grace now fills the house with the needy who come at God's call.
corruption_paragraphs: Some readings reduce the parable to an ethic of hospitality toward the marginalized. Hospitality is a Christian duty, but the parable's point is the gospel invitation: those who presumed on their privileges are shut out, and the feast is given to those who know their need.

The parable also shows God's sovereign purpose: my house shall be filled. The urgency of the servant is the urgency of gospel preaching, and the guests are brought in by the master's call. Churches should carry the invitation into the lanes respectable religion overlooks.

pos: v. (past tense; rolled over and over; fell headlong)
etymology: From Middle English tumblen, frequentative of tumben, to dance or leap, from Old English tumbian. The Hebrew means to turn over or roll.
biblical_def: Gideon had reduced his army to three hundred men at the LORD's command, and the Midianites lay along the valley like grasshoppers for multitude. To strengthen his faith, God sent him down to the enemy camp by night, where he overheard a soldier telling a dream: “Behold, I dreamed a dream, and, lo, a cake of barley bread tumbled into the host of Midian, and came unto a tent, and smote it that it fell, and overturned it, that the tent lay along.” His companion interpreted it at once: “This is nothing else save the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, a man of Israel: for into his hand hath God delivered Midian, and all the host” (Judges 7:14). Barley bread was the food of the poor, a fitting image for Gideon's small, despised force. Yet the humble loaf overturned the tent. Gideon worshipped and returned to rally his men. The account teaches that God chooses the weak things of the world to confound the mighty (1 Corinthians 1:27), so that no flesh should glory in His presence. The victory was won with trumpets, pitchers and lamps, and the cry, “The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon.”

The church is constantly tempted to trust numbers, resources and influence. Gideon's barley cake rebukes that trust. God delights to work through what the world despises, the foolishness of preaching and the weakness of His people, so that no flesh should glory in His presence.

etymology: From Middle English snacchen, to seize suddenly, related to Middle Dutch snakken, to gasp. The Hebrew gazar means to cut or divide, to tear off.
biblical_def: Isaiah describes the northern kingdom under God's judgment, consumed by its own wickedness as a fire devours briers and thorns: “And he shall snatch on the right hand, and be hungry; and he shall eat on the left hand, and they shall not be satisfied: they shall eat every man the flesh of his own arm.” The picture is of a famine of the soul so extreme that men grab at everything around them and are never filled, until they turn on their own kindred. The next verse names it: “Manasseh, Ephraim; and Ephraim, Manasseh: and they together shall be against Judah” (Isaiah 9:21). Brother tribes devoured one another. This is the self-destroying nature of sin left to itself; God's judgment is often simply giving men over to the consequences of their own lusts (Romans 1:24). The refrain of the passage is chilling: “For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.” Yet the same chapter contains the great promise of the Child born and the Son given, whose government and peace shall have no end (Isaiah 9:6-7). Only His reign can end the snatching hunger of the human heart.

Isaiah's picture fits every society that has abandoned God: endless grasping, unsatisfied appetite, and finally brother turning against brother. Political and economic remedies cannot cure it. The answer Isaiah gives in the same chapter is the Child born, the Prince of Peace, whose government alone brings lasting peace.

pos: adj. (congealed by cold; turned to ice)
etymology: From Old English froren, past participle of freosan, to freeze. The Hebrew means to be caught or held fast together.
biblical_def: When the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind, He questioned him about the wonders of creation that no man can explain or command: “Out of whose womb came the ice? and the hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it? The waters are hid as with a stone, and the face of the deep is frozen” (Job 38:29-30). The water that flows freely becomes hard as stone, the face of the deep held fast by cold. Job could not explain it, still less cause it. The purpose of God's questions was not to give Job a lesson in physics but to bring him to see the majesty of the Creator and his own smallness. The psalmist echoes the same truth: “He giveth snow like wool: he scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes. He casteth forth his ice like morsels: who can stand before his cold? He sendeth out his word, and melteth them” (Psalm 147:16-18). The frozen deep is a sign of God's sovereign power over every part of creation, and of His word that can both bind and loose. Even the winter is His.

etymology: From well and favoured, from favour in its old sense of appearance or countenance, from Latin favor. The Hebrew means good of grace, comely.
biblical_def: Nahum's prophecy against Nineveh describes the city's violence and then names the root of its corruption: “Because of the multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms, and families through her witchcrafts.” Nineveh is pictured as a beautiful, seductive harlot who used her charm, her trade and her occult arts to enslave nations and families. Her attractiveness was her weapon. The LORD's answer is immediate: “Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts; and I will discover thy skirts upon thy face, and I will shew the nations thy nakedness, and the kingdoms thy shame” (Nahum 3:5). The beauty that seduced would be stripped away to expose the corruption underneath. The image anticipates Babylon the great in Revelation 17, “THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH,” with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication. Worldly power and culture often present themselves as wellfavoured, attractive and sophisticated, yet they draw nations away from God. Scripture warns believers not to be seduced by the outward beauty of a system that God has judged.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): WELL-FAVORED, handsome; well formed; beautiful; pleasing to the eye.
webster_full: WELL-FAVORED, a. Handsome; well formed; beautiful; pleasing to the eye.
FAVOR, n. (obsolete sense) Countenance; appearance; as, a man of good favor.
Nahum 3:4 calls Nineveh the wellfavoured harlot and mistress of witchcrafts.
She sold nations through her whoredoms and families through her witchcrafts.
The LORD of hosts declares Himself against her (Nahum 3:5).
scriptures: Nah 3:4

Nah 3:5
Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts; and I will discover thy skirts upon thy face, and I will shew the nations thy nakedness, and the kingdoms thy shame.
Rev 17:5
And upon her forehead was a name written, MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.
corruption_summary: The attractive face of worldly culture and power is admired uncritically, while its idolatry, sorcery and enslaving influence over nations and families go unnamed.
corruption_paragraphs: Nineveh was beautiful, wealthy and culturally dominant, and its very attractiveness made its corruption effective. Modern culture likewise presents itself in sophisticated and appealing forms, while drawing families and nations away from God through its entertainments, commerce and false spiritualities.

Scripture calls believers to see through the wellfavoured face. The LORD is against every harlot city, and He will expose its shame. Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins (Revelation 18:4).
roots_summary: Well and favour, appearance; Nahum 3:4 names Nineveh the wellfavoured harlot.
